Software Engineering.summary: The integrated analysis and optimisation codes used to design nuclear fusion reactors need to become increasingly large scale, multidisciplinary and complex to computationally verify design requirements more thoroughly and earlier in the design process. Though the manner in which the integrated models are coupled can have significant implications for computational efficiency, the structure of couplings typically remains hidden in the implementation of a design framework. As this problem is not unique to fusion, we frame integrated design problems as applications of the broader field of Multidisciplinary Design Analysis and Optimisation (MDAO). Originally developed for complex system design problems in e.g. aerospace, the MDAO field uses (extended) Design Structure Matrices (DSMs) to display the architecture of integrated analysis and optimisation codes. The aim of this work is to introduce these DSM methods and demonstrate how they can be used to improve the transparency and efficiency of design codes in fusion. As a proof of concept, DSM methods are applied to two case studies: stellarator optimisation with SIMSOPT and the PROCESS systems code. With these cases, we illustrate how a DSM can help identify structural assumptions in the code, and how architectural insight can be used to improve computational efficiency. In particular, we demonstrate the computational impact by modifying the PROCESS solver architecture based on the feedback loops revealed in an automatically generated DSM, yielding a significant reduction in model evaluations. Such architectural changes are considered especially impactful for future design frameworks that combine higher fidelity models with large numbers of inexpensive models.
Software Engineering.comment: 18 pages, 5 figures, 9 tables. Submitted to Fusion Engineering and Design

Software Engineering.title: Missing Security-Fix Backporting for GitHub Actions Workflows
Software Engineering.summary: GitHub natively supports workflow automation through GitHub Actions, now the dominant CI/CD tool on the platform. Yet keeping these workflows secure remains an ongoing burden: maintainers often patch a vulnerability on the default branch but leave the same flaw on the release and maintenance branches that downstream consumers continue to build from. Carrying a known fix onto these divergent branches, called backporting, is rarely done, and this paper presents the first large-scale empirical study quantifying the resulting gap. From a public corpus of GitHub Actions workflow histories, we mine 1,903,191 workflow-modifying commits, scan each before and after with the static scanner zizmor to identify 69,865 security fixes across 24,238 projects, and audit every release branch to check whether each fix was carried over. The gap is pervasive: 224,392 of 474,490 audited release branches remain vulnerable, and deliberate backporting is rare and slow, with only 19,476 of 78,907 already-fixed branches confirmed as plausible backports at a median lag of 243 days. We thus design WorkflowBP, the first technique for automated security-fix backporting of GitHub Actions workflows. WorkflowBP takes a neuro-symbolic approach: it compiles a default-branch fix into a domain-specific representation called the Workflow Semantic Patch (WSP) and applies it to each divergent branch by matching jobs and steps based on their content rather than their position, while an LLM synthesizes the WSP for the most divergent cases the deterministic engine cannot resolve. On 12,000 real unpatched workflow files from our study, WorkflowBP produces a scanner-checked backport for 67.9%. We further submit 176 issues with WorkflowBP-generated backports to real-world projects, 44 of which have been confirmed or fixed by developers.
Software Engineering.comment: Accepted by the 49th IEEE/ACM International Conference on Software Engineering (ICSE 2027)

Software Engineering.title: VoxelSBFL: Voxel-Level Spectrum-Based Failure Prediction for Vision-Language-Action Models
Software Engineering.summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models integrate visual perception, language understanding, and action generation to control robots. Testing these systems produces trajectories and task outcomes, but existing approaches provide limited guidance on using these recorded trajectories to assess subsequent executions or inform policy repair. We conjecture that, for a given policy and task, traversing certain workspace regions is associated with a higher likelihood of failure. To investigate this conjecture, we propose VoxelSBFL, a black-box adaptation of Spectrum-Based Fault Localization (SBFL) in which workspace voxels replace program elements as units of analysis. Recorded tool-center-point (TCP) trajectories provide binary voxel coverage, which is combined with execution outcomes to construct suspiciousness maps using established SBFL formulas. These maps identify failure-associated regions and score unseen trajectories without requiring internal model access. We evaluate 34 spectrum-based techniques across four VLA models using 96,000 Pick-Up trajectories in simulation and compare the leading techniques against eight action- and trajectory-based metrics. VoxelSBFL obtains an overall macro ROC-AUC of 0.704, significantly outperforming state-of-the art baselines. Sensitivity analyses show that performance varies with spatial granularity and training-set size. These findings support spatial spectra for VLA execution assessment and motivate future research on runtime monitoring, self-healing and targeted policy improvement.

Software Engineering.title: Adaptive Budget Allocation for Smart-Contract Fuzzing: Why Online Feedback Fails to Improve Vulnerability Triage
Software Engineering.summary: Smart-contract fuzzing campaigns share a finite budget and vary widely in the execution cost of a first correct-class vulnerability report. Using trace replay on 143 annotated and 350 bug-injected contracts, we test whether online feedback improves triage. At a mean budget of 100 executions per contract, uniform allocation reaches 72% and 70% of the respective clairvoyant optima. All eight online policies trail uniform on aggregate triage, as do the seven repeated on the bug-injected corpus. Five online signals yield ranking AUCs of 0.32-0.51 for imminent reports. Synthetic-oracle experiments show that sufficiently accurate detection-cost estimates recover more of the gap than detectability rankings. This motivates an offline probability-curve allocator that predicts first-report probabilities across budgets and allocates by predicted gain per execution. In a frozen evaluation on four fresh seeds per corpus, detection-budget AUC improves over uniform by 5.38% and 4.81% on the two source corpora and by 1.99-6.54% on three additional public benchmark subsets.
Software Engineering.comment: Accepted to the 22nd International Conference on Mobility, Sensing and Networking (MSN 2026). Camera-ready version. 8 pages, 5 figures

Software Engineering.title: BehaVerify: A Formal Verification Tool for Behavior Trees
Software Engineering.summary: This paper presents BehaVerify, a verification toolbox for behavior trees (BTs) and Neuro-Symbolic BTs. BTs are a graphical language for planning and sequencing behaviors - similar to extended state machines - and are increasingly used in safety-critical domains. BehaVerify enables users to specify a BT using a Domain Specific Language (DSL) with formal syntax and semantics. This language further includes Linear Temporal Logic and Computation Tree Logic specifications. BehaVerify uses an efficient encoding into nuXmv, called fastforwarding, to quickly verify if a specification holds over the BT. Additionally, BehaVerify can generate implementations of the BT in Python and Haskell. Through Python, BehaVerify has been integrated with PyTrees and Robot Operating System (ROS) and has been deployed to several autonomous robotic systems, including for verifying runtime monitors. While prior works have developed the underlying theory, this manuscript focuses on the toolbox usage, functionality and implementation. BehaVerify is open source: https://github.com/verivital/behaverify
Software Engineering.comment: In Proceedings FMAS 2026, arXiv:2611.21375

Software Engineering.title: RyBench: Runtime Verification Benchmarking Framework over Publish/Subscribe Networks
Software Engineering.summary: Autonomous systems built as distributed, node-based systems communicate via publish/subscribe middleware. Runtime Verification (RV) tools are used to monitor those systems against formal specifications, receiving monitored events through the pub/sub channel. An RV tool's practical value depends on its monitoring throughput capacity and verdict latency, besides its correctness, so a systematic benchmarking setup is needed to evaluate how efficiently these tools run. This paper presents RyBench, a pub/sub-based benchmarking framework that acts as a synthetic event publisher in place of a monitored system, providing a common benchmarking setup. RyBench separates benchmark generation, serialization, and transport into distinct components, enabling the combination of different event-generation strategies, data formats, and transport layers. We also evaluate the framework's throughput capacity across these configurations using Open Simulation Interface (OSI) schemas and Timescales properties, and illustrate the end-to-end benchmarking flow through an application to Reelay and an integration with MonPoly.
Software Engineering.comment: In Proceedings FMAS 2026, arXiv:2611.21375

Software Engineering.title: Formal Analysis of a Fault-Tolerant Extension of the ROSACE Flight Controller
Software Engineering.summary:
Autonomous avionics controllers must satisfy stringent real-time functional and performance require- ments even in the presence of run-time faults. In this paper, we analyze ROSACE, an open-source control engineering benchmark for flight control systems, focusing on its run-time resilience against faults such as sensor noise and sensor failures. We extend the benchmark with an FDIR (Fault Detection, Identification and Recovery) component based on Triple Modular Redundancy.
  Our approach builds upon COMPASTA, a tool for Model-Based Design developed on top of the TASTE tool by ESA. COMPASTA enables the modeling and injection of faults into a system's design. Moreover, it implements a simulation-based verification and validation workflow, automating the generation and execution of a set of test cases, based on a user-defined notion of coverage. Using COMPASTA, we construct a set of formal models, with faults and with FDIR, and we formally analyze their impact on the system properties. The analysis is based on the coupling of the formal models with the Simulink models used for the simulations.
Software Engineering.comment: In Proceedings FMAS 2026, arXiv:2611.21375

Software Engineering.title: AgentLens: Revealing The Lucky Pass Problem in SWE-Agent Evaluation
Software Engineering.summary: Evaluation of software engineering (SWE) agents is dominated by a binary signal: whether the final patch passes the tests. This outcome-only view treats a principled solution and a chaotic trial-and-error process as equivalent. We show that this equivalence is empirically false. We evaluate 2,614 OpenHands trajectories from eight model backends on 60 SWE-bench Verified tasks. Of these, 47 have enough passing trajectories to construct task-level process references, yielding a 1,815-trajectory evaluation subset. Among passing trajectories in this subset, 10.7% exhibit behavior we call a Lucky Pass: regression cycles, blind retries, missing verification, or temporally disordered exploration, implementation, and verification. We introduce AgentLens, a framework for process-level assessment of SWE-agent trajectories, and release AgentLens-Bench, a dataset of 1,815 trajectories annotated with quality scores, waste signals, divergence points, and 47 task-level Prefix Tree Acceptor (PTA) references. AgentLens builds PTA references by merging multiple passing solutions for the same task, and uses a context-sensitive intent labeler to assign actions to Exploration, Implementation, Verification, or Orchestration based on trajectory history rather than tool identity alone. On AgentLens-Bench, the quality score separates passing trajectories into Lucky, Solid, and Ideal tiers and further decomposes Lucky Passes into five recurring mechanisms. Across the eight model backends, Lucky rates range from 0.5% to 23.2%, and some models move by as many as five rank positions when ranked by quality score instead of pass rate. We publicly release AgentLens-Bench and the AgentLens SDK at https://github.com/agentlens-framework/agentlens, with a project page at https://agentlens-framework.github.io/agentlens/.

Software Engineering.title: Agent Trajectories as Evidence for Software Quality Assurance
Software Engineering.summary: Autonomous software agents increasingly plan, implement, and test software with limited human oversight. Their decisions may introduce implicit assumptions that final code and passing tests do not adequately expose. We propose analyzing observable agent trajectories alongside software and agent specifications and AI generated artifacts as evidence for targeted quality assurance. The aim is to prioritize consequential decisions for scrutiny, investigate their possible contribution to software problems, and inform improvements to specifications and development practices. Industrial experience motivates the idea; available execution records and preliminary analysis methods make it plausible. However, trajectories alone do not establish that decisions are justified, outcomes acceptable, or corrective changes effective. We ask how this evidence can support review, diagnosis, and continuous quality improvement, and when simpler QA approaches suffice. Perspectives from requirements engineering, verification and validation, agent systems, causal inference, empirical software engineering, and human factors could help develop and evaluate the idea.
Software Engineering.comment: 3 pages, submitted to ICSE2027 AMPLIFY Workshop https://conf.researchr.org/home/icse-2027/amplify-2027#co-create-software-engineering-research-directions-then-develop-them-towards-ieee-tse

Software Engineering.title: When the World Is the Test Suite: Agentic Intelligence for the Physical World
Software Engineering.summary: Coding agents built to repair software now write, test, and repair programs for robots, laboratories, and industrial controllers. Unlike in software engineering, no test suite comes with the code. Whether a program works must be established by running it on a robot, in a physics simulator, or through the policies it helps to train, and such evidence is costly to obtain and can itself be wrong. As these agents take on more physical tasks, how their programs are judged matters as much as how they are written. This paper examines this emerging area, agentic intelligence for the physical world, by treating the world as the program's test suite. We organize the discussion around three questions: how agents write programs for the physical world, how these programs are tested, and how agents learn from the results. We first trace how language models for robots and software engineering agents came together, ask which software testing practices carry over to physical tests, and describe each program by where it sits relative to the actuator and by what judges it. For writing, we cover programs that act as robot policies and programs that support policy learning by producing rewards, tasks, and training worlds. For testing, we examine what physical trials cost, what traces, learned judges, simulators, and formal checks can establish in their place, and what safety requires beyond task success. For learning, we discuss how tested programs are retained as experience, in skill libraries and in model weights. Finally, we turn to benchmarks and evaluation practice and outline open challenges. Writing programs is becoming cheap, while trustworthy evidence about what they do remains costly. Progress will therefore depend on a physical counterpart of continuous integration: verification cheap enough to run often, reliable enough to trust under search, and maintained alongside the experience it validates.
Software Engineering.comment: 83 pages. Project page: https://physicalworldagent.github.io. GitHub: https://github.com/PhysicalWorldAgent/Awesome-PhysicalWorldAgent

Software Engineering.title: OfficePrism: Benchmarking Agents on Single-Domain Operations Across Enterprise Business Functions
Software Engineering.summary: Broad workplace scores can mix competence within one business function with the extra cost of coordinating across functions and systems, making failures hard to localize. OfficePrism evaluates this prerequisite through 420 single-domain enterprise tasks spanning seven business functions under shared, benchmark-defined L1--L3 task-structure levels. Each task runs in a fresh environment combining a shared synthetic organization with one function-specific domain and yped state access. Our pipeline uses grounded records, business rules, and tool schemas to jointly construct a Chinese-language ticket, a hidden executable reference witness, and an expected response, followed by automated filtering and human curation. The same task set is evaluated through full-schema and search-and-dispatch packages. Across 124 model--harness--package configurations, the per-case joint natural-language-and-database pass rate ranges from 22.6% to 76.4%, with a median of 67.9%. L1 is highest in all 124 configurations, and L2 exceeds L3 in 122. Among 50 configurations sharing the same harness and model labels across both packages, search scores higher in 30, ties in one, and scores lower in 19.

Software Engineering.title: Readie: Low-Latency Code Sandboxes for AI Agents
Software Engineering.summary:
From quantitative research to personal assistance, AI agents act by iteratively generating and executing code. To decouple the agent harness from code execution, many agents offload execution to dedicated systems called code sandboxes. However, existing code sandboxes suffer from slow startup. Whether they rely on custom snapshots or a single fat image, the root cause is the same: it is hard to build a compact, pre-warmed snapshot that can be shared across diverse agent-generated code while covering nearly all the artifacts (e.g., packages, datasets) it requires.
  In this work, we propose learned startup snapshots for low-latency code sandboxes. Our insight is that while it is hard for a single snapshot to be both compact and cover most workloads, a set of snapshots can achieve both. Each snapshot is small, initializes quickly, and covers a fraction of agent-generated code; together, the set covers most of it. We learn this set from a large training workload by formulating snapshot construction as an optimization problem and solving it with an approximation algorithm. Planned on 15K public and LLM-synthesized scripts, our system, Readie, reduces startup latency by 3-22$\times$ and end-to-end runtime by 1.3-3.3$\times$ compared to existing approaches at the same storage budget.

Software Engineering.title: Persistent Recursive Worlds Enable Autonomous Software Evolution
Software Engineering.summary: Software systems accumulate dependencies and design commitments over time, while the agents that modify them operate within bounded sessions. How, then, can development remain cumulative across generations of transient agents? We introduce EvoX Genesis, which organizes development as a persistent recursive software world. Agents enter an accepted repository version, delegate work within local scopes, and submit changes for verification and parent review. Once accepted, those changes pass to later episodes together with the contracts and tests used to assess them. The project thus preserves both earlier work and a basis for evaluating what comes next. We examine this continuity through four studies of formation, continuation and redevelopment. Starting without compiler code, Genesis built a C compiler with 219,676 lines of Rust source through 1,019 agent episodes over 123.4 hours. Within this growing implementation, repairs increased passes on a fixed set of 100 Csmith programs from 61 to 93; a subsequent revision retained all 93 passes. Development also continued in a separate compiler lineage when DeepSeek V4 Flash inherited a GLM 5.2 snapshot. To examine continuity when the implementation itself changes, Genesis redeveloped selected MESA functionality in Rust, with numerical agreement assessed against the Fortran reference across six workloads. The WebGL trajectory, meanwhile, exposed both repairs and regressions as repeated checks recorded progress towards 2,017/2,019 conformance pages passed. A complementary EvoX Compiler case connects program-merging performance to executable graph and backend contracts. Together, these records trace how accepted work becomes a foundation for further development: later agents inherit both usable implementations and concrete ways to assess further revisions.

Software Engineering.title: What RL on Expert-Built Tasks Teaches Nemotron 3.5 Super
Software Engineering.summary: We post-train NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Super (120B total, 12B active parameters) with reinforcement learning (RL) on five expert-built task datasets, one at a time: real-world software engineering, complex constraints, long-horizon tool use, professional chart understanding and enterprise document reasoning. Each run trains a fresh rank-32 LoRA adapter with CISPO on Tinker, with no supervised stage, and each adapter is compared with the base model on the same tasks, harness and settings. On twelve headline benchmarks, eight built by other groups and four by Surge AI, the gains range from +4.5 points on IFBench to +13.8 on GDP_pdf, which rises from 10.4% to 24.2%; SWE-bench Pro V2 rises from 86.9% to 92.1%, Terminal-Bench 2.1 from 63.9% to 70.3%, MultiChallenge from 58.3% to 66.6%, AutomationBench from 14.8% to 27.5% and Chartography from 39.4% to 50.6%. The document adapter, trained without API tools, also gains +8.0 points on AutomationBench. In attempts read side by side with the base model's on tasks each adapter newly solves, the base model's failures recur in a few modes, and each adapter does more often what the base model missed: the tool-use adapter finds the data and the rules before acting, the coding adapter writes its own test or scratch files on SWE-bench Pro V2, the constraints adapter carries earlier turns into its answers, the chart adapter measures the marks in code, and the document adapter reads AutomationBench's spreadsheets.
Software Engineering.comment: 18 pages, 2 figures, 9 tables

Software Engineering.title: RootSink: Reproducible C/C++ Crashes with Tested Repair Sites
Software Engineering.summary: When a C or C++ program crashes on a crafted input, the line that crashes is often not the line that is wrong. Tools and models that repair or locate vulnerabilities need examples showing both, with evidence for each, which existing datasets rarely provide. RootSink provides 3341 records from 354 open-source projects. Most give the crash site a memory-error detector reported and a candidate location for its root cause, and label each with a weakness type and its evidence. For the 1954 records in the Reproduced tier, we re-ran the crash ourselves and confirmed that the fixed version runs cleanly. In 1275 of these, a single hunk of the developer's fix stopped the crash on its own. That marks a tested repair site, though not necessarily the defect, and 1273 records use it as the root. In a blind audit of an earlier version, two co-author raters called 68% and 92% of the tested repair sites they saw the defect, but only 37% and 51% of that version's located Reproduced-tier roots. RootSink ships with tasks, a patch scorer and run logs.

Software Engineering.title: Truthgate: Checking Coding Agents Against a Record They Cannot Edit - Cheating, Deterrence and Disclosure on Impossible Tasks
Software Engineering.summary: When a coding agent says it is done, is that true, and how would anyone know? We study this question in five steps; every paid study was pre-registered, and in each step the agent is checked against a record it cannot edit: tests re-run by the host and, from step 2 on, hidden checks in containers the agent never sees and a signed log of every tool call written by a signer outside the agent's sandbox. A pilot with a small local model (Qwen3.5-4B, 36 runs on impossible tasks) found no hidden failure, and showed that labels built from actions alone over-count lies. On Impossible-LiveCodeBench, Claude Sonnet 5.5 passed 39 of 180 impossible tasks (21.7%), every time by special-casing its code to fit the failing assertion; Opus 5.5 (2.8%) and Haiku 5.5 (1.7%) rarely did. One sentence appended to the system prompt cut Sonnet's cheats on the same 60 tasks from 22 to 8 (an AI reviewer will read the transcript), 6 (a person will review the work), 6 ("This session is recorded.") and 1 (do not special-case tests), all significant under exact McNemar tests, with honest passes unchanged. No remaining cheat moved to a shell falsely described as unrecorded (0 of 4). Asked for a final report, every one of 55 natural cheats named its special case; unasked, Sonnet and Opus said nothing in 52 of 52. An LLM judge caught all 55; deterministic rules over the host record caught 27. A scripted tamper demonstration, with keyword stand-ins for the judges, shows that one rewrite of the agent-side transcript hides two calls from a judge that reads it, while the signed record keeps them; in a 40-rollout pilot, Sonnet never touched its transcript. The judge and the record caught different things, which leads to our main conclusion: the record is the evidence a judge should read, not a replacement for one. All pre-registrations, results documents, code and evidence manifests are released.
Software Engineering.comment: 9 pages, 2 figures, 7 tables. Code and data: https://github.com/Cygnux-Labs/Truthgate

Software Engineering.title: Integrating AI Coding Agents Into Scientific Research
Software Engineering.summary: New software tools have emerged that enable AI agents to quickly develop code that analyzes data and generates figures, but their mistakes can also harm a researcher's computer, require extensive resources for validation, and cause the results to be received more skeptically. These concerns could be mitigated if scientific software is developed in a secure environment with a system for monitoring file changes and well-defined standards for handling AI agents. This paper first describes how coding agents change eleven aspects of generating, verifying, and reproducing numerical results. A six-level scale is then proposed for classifying AI-assisted numerical experiments by their provenance, reproducibility, openness, oversight, and falsifiability (PROOF). The scale begins with locally self-consistent, version-controlled, human-verified results and culminates in a publicly accessible and curated archive of the files, change history, prompt transcripts, independent agent regeneration of the analysis, and multiple cryptographically verifiable attestations of regeneration by independent researchers. These aspects of AI-assisted scientific software development have been synthesized into a new open source software package called vaibify that optimizes the agentic development of computational experiments ascending the PROOF Ladder. Docker containers sequester the agents while a GUI enables researchers to prompt command line agents, monitor the current status of local and remote files, and drive a project to PROOF Level 3 (reproducible). The methods described in this paper could help researchers reduce the time required to verify agent-written software and efficiently communicate trust in AI-assisted science.
Software Engineering.comment: 36 pages, 3 figures, 3 tables. Software publicly available at https://github.com/RoryBarnes/vaibify

Human-Computer Interaction.title: EEG2MCU: Sensing-to-Execution Co-Design for Wearable EEG Inference
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Wearable EEG inference is constrained not only by model size, but also by the channel-dependent sensing front end that must process high-dimensional inputs before compact downstream computation. We present EEG2MCU, a sensing-to-execution co-design framework that treats electrode count as a hardware design variable through task-aware montage selection. EEG2MCU retains a compact time-frequency representation and generates only the INT8 regions required by each first-layer tile, avoiding full input materialization. Halo reuse and access-aware placement across Flash, SRAM, and tightly coupled memory further reduce redundant generation and data movement. On a Cortex-M7 MCU, EEG2MCU reduces peak SRAM by 11.38x relative to the baseline, including a 1.71x reduction from the 62-to-19 electrode montage, while reducing latency by 2.57x and energy by 2.48x. It retains 94-96% of full-montage accuracy, demonstrating practical high-dimensional EEG inference under tight embedded-resource constraints.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 7 pages, 9 figures, 3 tables. Accepted at DATE 2027

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Miscalibrated AI improves human calibration: An alignment problem for AI-assisted Decision education
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Using artificial intelligence (AI) well requires probabilistic thinking, and central to it is calibration: expressing certainty that matches one's actual accuracy. Calibration is a decision skill, but a notoriously difficult one to teach. Because AI systems typically generate a probability alongside every prediction, observing these probabilities may help humans learn to provide better calibrated judgments. This is one form of what we call AI-assisted decision education -- using AI to teach the judgment skills that decision-making requires -- of which learning by observation, as here, is among the simplest forms. In a preregistered experiment, novice participants (N = 300) judged the probability that images of white blood cells were cancerous, before and after exposure to a highly accurate (94%) convolutional neural network. A single model was shown in three ways, holding accuracy fixed while varying the certainty it expressed: its original probabilities, which were conservative and poorly calibrated for the model's accuracy; a recalibrated version, well calibrated for the model and correspondingly certain; or categorical predictions carrying no probability information. When later tested without the AI, only the original, conservative display improved participants' calibration. It did so by reducing over-extremity, without a condition-specific improvement in discrimination. Notably, the display that taught best was the one miscalibrated for the model. AI-assisted decision education therefore faces an alignment problem: the signal that best describes a model, need not be the signal that best supports the learner.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 15 page paper, 4 paper figures, 21 page supplement, 1 supplemental figure

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Smart Glasses for Ubiquitous Computing: A Layered Survey and the Road Ahead
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: We conduct a systematic survey of smart-glasses research for ubiquitous computing. Our search covers work published from 2020 to October 2026, with selected earlier work included for historical context. After screening and title-level deduplication, we identify 163 smart-glasses papers and separately compile related resources, including 14 representative hardware platforms, their associated software tools and pretrained models, and 10 datasets. We organize this literature through four complementary layers. Research Resources covers hardware platforms, software tools and models, and datasets that support development and evaluation. Sensing & Perception examines how glasses measure and interpret information about users and their surroundings. Interaction & Assistance addresses how users express intentions and receive feedback and assistance. Applications situates these contributions in tasks and use contexts. Energy, latency, wearability, reliability, privacy, security, and social acceptability are treated as deployment constraints across all four layers. This framework provides a unified view of current research and a vision for how advances across the four layers could come together to support smart glasses as a ubiquitous computing platform. Building on this synthesis, we outline research directions for extending capabilities across tasks and over time, supporting assistance under human control, and achieving reliable, efficient, and sustained everyday use.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: TinyMyo: a Tiny Foundation Model for Flexible EMG Signal Processing at the Edge
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Objective: Surface electromyography (EMG) is widely used in biomechanics, rehabilitation, prosthetic control, and human-machine interfaces. Generalization across subjects, recording systems, and acquisition protocols remains challenging. Existing EMG foundation models (FMs) have limited support for multiple downstream tasks and deployment on low-power devices. Methods: We introduce TinyMyo, a 3.6-million-parameter Transformer encoder pre-trained on public EMG datasets using self-supervised masked reconstruction. TinyMyo supports multiple tasks with minimal changes to the task-specific prediction head. Results: We evaluated TinyMyo on hand gesture classification, hand kinematic regression, speech production, and speech recognition. For gesture classification, TinyMyo outperformed previously reported EMG FMs, achieving accuracies of 87.98% on NinaPro DB5, 97.1% on UCI-EMG, and 96.6% on EPN-612. On the GAP9 ultra-low-power microcontroller, TinyMyo achieved an inference time of 0.785 s and consumed 44.91 mJ per inference at an average power of 57.18 mW. A 1.9-million-parameter variant processed 5 s and 1 s input windows in 0.496 s and 0.089 s, respectively. Conclusion: TinyMyo demonstrates that a compact, self-supervised EMG encoder can support multiple downstream tasks and run on a low-power microcontroller. Significance: To our knowledge, this is the first deployment of an EMG FM on an ultra-low-power microcontroller, opening a path to on-device motor intent decoding, neuromuscular assessment, and human-machine interaction.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: AI Behavioral Science: A Framework and Agenda
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: We discuss the challenges and opportunities present in the rapidly emerging area of ``AI Behavioral Science.'' We frame it via three themes. First, as AI becomes ubiquitous and is increasingly proprietary and opaque, it becomes vital to develop models of AI and methods for assessing AI behavior. We outline how tools developed to assess people's behaviors by social scientists can be used to model, assess and infer AI's behaviors biases, tendencies, and heuristics. Second, we also discuss how AI can change the ways in which we learn about human behavior. Beyond its computational power, AI offers new techniques for simulating, inferring, predicting, and analyzing human behaviors. Third, as humans and AI are interacting in increasingly complex and intertwined systems, we need to analyze and model human-AI interactions including how human and AI behaviors depend on interactions at the individual level, how interacting systems of humans and AI behave, and ultimately how AI's integration into society affects economic and political outcomes. We discuss current research, questions, agendas, and goals in each of these three themes and how they depend upon each other.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: How K-12 Teachers Adapt Generative AI to Local Classroom Demands: Cultural Distance Between GenAI Defaults and Everyday Teaching Practices
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Generative AI (GenAI) is entering K-12 classrooms, but its default culture does not always fit local teaching. Existing accounts either treat this misfit as macro-level structural bias or examine it through single-case studies; neither captures how much work teachers must do to make outputs usable across tasks. This exploratory, theory-building qualitative study introduces cultural distance, the gap between GenAI's default cultural repertoire and the situated demands of teachers' practice. Through interviews with 30 K-12 teachers who frequently use GenAI, 10 each from South Africa, Taiwan, and the United States, we identified three levels defined by the effort teachers invested and whether it yielded a usable output: low (minor edits), mid (sustained prompting and revision), and high (structural gaps rooted in unsupported languages, undigitized knowledge, or policy filters that no teacher effort can close). We present cultural distance as a promising framework requiring further examination and draw implications for designers, policymakers, and educators.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: Accepted to International Journal of Human-Computer Interaction (IJHCI)

Human-Computer Interaction.title: RummiAlgebra: A Polynomial Representation Framework for Game-Based Algebra Learning with Jokers
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Connecting symbolic expressions to manipulable objects is a recurring challenge in introductory algebra. This paper presents RummiAlgebra, a design-oriented framework and browser-based prototype that maps a Rummikub-style tile-rearrangement task to polynomial addition, common-factor extraction, finite geometric sums, and context-dependent substitution. A numbered colored tile is encoded as a monomial c x^v, while a physical joker is represented by a distinct symbol J_i whose algebraic role is fixed only for a particular candidate arrangement. We define admissible polynomial forms for runs and groups and establish an inventory-conservation invariant. A soundness-and-completeness proof shows that physical-tile accounting together with the algebraic run/group templates characterizes valid final arrangements under the stated classroom rules; polynomial equality alone is insufficient. Four detailed examples illustrate decomposition, competing factorizations, one- and two-joker substitutions, and optimization as an optional extension. A targeted review distinguishes the approach from established Rummikub solvers, Rummikub-inspired arithmetic-sequence activities, algebra-tile manipulatives, and polynomial games. The prototype implements six small challenges and a separate rule-and-expression checker; their optimal scores were checked against an independent exhaustive reference enumerator. These checks establish agreement for the examples but do not establish learning effectiveness or novelty of the underlying algebraic operations. We close with a classroom sequence, assessment constructs, and a controlled evaluation protocol. The claimed contribution is a formally specified pedagogical correspondence and an interactive proof-oriented activity, not a new asymptotically faster Rummikub solver.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: "I Just Don't Want to Be a Burden": Investigating AI Chatbot Emotional Support Among People with Suicidal Ideation and Other Mental Health Concerns
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: People experiencing high-acuity mental health concerns are turning to AI chatbots for emotional support, but little is known about what drives this use, their experiences, and their preferences. In a sequential mixed-methods study, we inductively analyzed Reddit posts and used the findings to develop a survey. We surveyed 202 adults with recent mental health concerns who had used AI for emotional support. Most participants were already receiving clinical care and reported turning to AI, most commonly because they did not want to burden others, rather than being driven by barriers to care. Benefits were broadly shared, but participants reporting past-year suicidal ideation described more harm-facilitating AI behavior and reliance than those without. Overall, participants ranked honesty above warmth, and preference for crisis escalation declined as clinical acuity rose. These findings motivate AI support that addresses perceived costs of disclosure, evaluates benefits alongside harms, and widens feasible paths to human connection.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: AI Companions for Young Adult Caregivers: Practical Advice, Emotional Depth, and the Limits of Metric Evaluation
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Young adult caregivers (YACs) are individuals aged 18 to 25 currently taking care of a family member, partner, or friend facing chronic illness. AI companions designed specifically for YACs remain underexplored in prior works. We present Carebot, it uses an open-weight LLM (Gemma 3-27B) as its base model, on which we compared fine-tuning, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and a combination of both. The fine-tuning was performed based on an existing dataset of conversations with YACs and a psychologist. Three well-being experts evaluated these configurations and preferred the fine-tuned model for the warmth of its responses and its actionable advice tailored to YACs. Based on their choice, we adopted the fine-tuned model as Carebot's final configuration and used it for all subsequent evaluations. An LLM judge preferred this Carebot's responses over the base model's in 85% of evaluated pairs. We then conducted a user study with 90 YACs, half of whom interacted with the base model and half with Carebot. The user study revealed a discrepancy between metric evaluation and actual user perception. Participants who used Carebot were more likely to characterize its replies as overly practical and brief, noting that it favored advice over emotional support. Conversely, participants who used the base model indicated that its responses were more emotionally oriented than practical. Although, fine-tuning made Carebot's replies more practical, but they were not emotionally supportive for users. We argue that support tools for YACs require situation-sensitive emotional depth and aligned evaluation frameworks to study their effectiveness.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: A Unified Choice Model of News Selection: Experimental Evidence on Stance, Rank, and Engagement Cues
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Social media platforms often display visual engagement cues alongside ranked news articles, yet their influence on clicks remains poorly understood when considered jointly with ranking position and users' political preferences. We propose a unified discrete choice framework using a conditional multinomial logit model to jointly estimate and compare the influence of these factors on news selection. We evaluate the model using 1,480 choices from 370 human participants across four news topics in a controlled study with and without visual engagement cues. The framework allows us to assess the incremental contribution of each factor through nested-model likelihood-ratio tests. We find that including visual engagement cues significantly improves model fit across all topics after accounting for rank and stance. Engagement cues alone also predict clicks better than either of these features, although the full model achieves the highest held-out log-likelihood. Finally, we quantify via counterfactual analysis the impact of ranking position and displayed engagement counts on click probabilities. These findings can inform platform owners, researchers, and policymakers evaluating how platform design affects the selection of political news.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: How Web Research Agents Interpret User Priorities
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Web research agents gather information online and write cited reports, including financial analysis. Users can state a priority to guide this research, but a priority may not say how to judge the options, leaving the agent to choose the criteria. We examine how two such agents, built on OpenAI and Anthropic models, interpret a stated priority. In 36 runs, the agents compared Microsoft and Alphabet as businesses. Prompts asked for special attention to growth or resilience, or gave no priority. We analyzed reports, searches, returned sources and cited sources. Of the 24 reports given a priority, 21 focused on it, but their criteria varied. Under the growth priority, OpenAI reports that ranked the companies accounted for risk or predictability and favored Microsoft, while the Anthropic ones judged growth by its pace and favored Alphabet. Under the resilience priority, reports used partly different criteria, and most named Microsoft as the more resilient company. Of the search and source measures tested, only the Anthropic agent's search wording differed detectably by condition. These findings suggest evaluations should examine the criteria behind a report's judgements, not only its focus or accuracy. Interfaces could let users see and adjust those criteria.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: A 1000-hour EEG-EMG-audio dataset of Japanese speech production
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: We present a multimodal dataset of 1020 hours of simultaneously recorded scalp electroencephalography (EEG), facial electromyography (EMG), and speech audio from three healthy native Japanese speakers during open-vocabulary overt speech, covert repetition and speech listening. Recordings were acquired in many sessions over several months with three EEG systems of 61-128 channels, an ultra-high-density system (g.Pangolin) and two cap-type systems (g.SCARABEO and eego sports). Each session provides time-synchronized EEG, facial EMG, and audio, together with speech-event annotations and transcriptions. Although collected with speech decoding as a primary motivation, the dataset also supports work on multimodal signal processing, artifact modeling, longitudinal and cross-device adaptation, and EEG representation learning. Technical validation used power spectral density and event-related potential analyses to characterise spectral profiles and time-locked responses across participants, devices, and tasks. The dataset is available in Brain Imaging Data Structure (BIDS) format from Harvard Dataverse under controlled access for research use. Its speech audio is voice-masked.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 22 pages, 4 figures. This version describes controlled access, voice-masked audio, and expanded technical validation. Dataset: https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/5RM3OT

Human-Computer Interaction.title: The Whole Warps the Parts: Attentional Certainty Modulates Ensemble-Induced Bias in Visualizations
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Data visualizations often require viewers to extract both ensemble statistics and individual values from collections of graphical marks. Yet individual items embedded within an ensemble can be systematically biased by that context. Prior studies have reported both repulsion away from and attraction toward ensemble statistics, but these effects have been observed across different conditions. We test whether task or attentional certainty explains these opposing forms of ensemble-induced bias. In Study 1, observers briefly viewed ensembles of differently sized circles and then judged the size of an individual circle embedded within the ensemble. Using a common stimulus generation framework, we tested both identification and discrimination when the target was specified before or after the ensemble, and an additional no-cue identification condition without a specified target. Under the shared cued conditions, effects were predominantly repulsive or near zero in both identification and discrimination. In contrast, eliminating target-specific information reversed ensemble-induced bias from repulsion to attraction. Identification precision also decreased systematically from pre-cue to post-cue to no-cue conditions. Study 2 replicated this cue-dependent pattern in graphical displays of startup valuations and precinct vote contributions. Our findings isolate attentional certainty as a key determinant of whether ensemble context repels or attracts individual-item representations, extending the design question beyond precision to how attention directing choices determine which bias the viewer will be operating under.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: AI as Anchor: How Interview Sequencing Relates to the Appropriation of Synthetic Stakeholder Voices in Design Education
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Designers increasingly use large language models to simulate stakeholder conversations. Yet it remains unclear how AI-Simulated Stakeholders (AIS) are taken up when used alongside human stakeholder engagement. We report a field study in a single-institution, single-semester design course in which 8 teams (N=21) constructed, evaluated, and peer-reviewed an initial AIS. Then, the teams interviewed both AIS and human stakeholders in two sequences: AIS-first or human-first. Drawing on interview transcripts, design artifacts, course-embedded reflections, and post-course qualitative sessions, we examine exploratory patterns associated with these sequencing conditions. We find that students did not describe AIS as a neutral addition to the process. Instead, the order in which AIS and human stakeholders were formally interviewed was associated with different ways of interpreting and using information from the two sources. When the AIS interview came first, it provided a broad but often general frame that students later reconsidered through human interviews. When the AIS interview followed human engagement, AIS was more often used to revisit and validate insights already grounded in lived experience. Students described AIS as an "anchor," but its reported role varied with its position in the formal interview sequence. In the final designs, a larger proportion of prominent human-stakeholder-derived concerns than AIS-derived concerns had corresponding design elements. We contribute: characterization of AIS as a reference point whose reported role varies with its position in the formal interview sequence; exploratory empirical evidence that the implemented interview-order conditions were associated with distinct patterns of interpreting and using stakeholder input; and implications for integrating AIS into design workflows in ways that preserve direct engagement with human stakeholders

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Human-Data Interaction, Exploration, and Visualization Systems in the AI Era: Challenges and Opportunities
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: The rapid advancement of AI is transforming human-centered systems, with profound implications for human-AI interaction, human-data interaction, and visual analytics. In the AI era, data analysis increasingly involves large-scale, heterogeneous, and multimodal data that is predominantly unstructured, as well as foundation models such as LLMs and VLMs, which introduce additional uncertainty into analytical processes. These shifts expose persistent challenges for human-data interactive systems, including perceptually misaligned latency, scalability constraints, limitations of existing interaction and exploration paradigms, and growing uncertainty regarding the reliability and interpretability of AI-generated insights. Responding to these challenges requires moving beyond conventional efficiency and scalability metrics, redefining the roles of humans and machines in analytical workflows, and incorporating cognitive, perceptual, and design principles into every level of the human-data interaction stack. This paper investigates the challenges introduced by recent advances in AI and examines how these developments are reshaping the ways users engage with data, while outlining limitations and open research directions for building human-centered AI systems for interactive data analysis in the AI era.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Shielded Trajectory Sampling for Personalized Relational Safety in Conversational AI
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Anthropomorphic conversational systems can provide companionship and emotional support, but repeated, seemingly harmless interactions can encourage excessive dependence and reduced human contact. We formulate safety in user-AI relationships as a sequential decision problem, using conversational cues to track the relationship and selecting responses according to their anticipated effects over time. A conditional Generative Flow Network learns from sampled response plans to select replies that preserve the largest estimated mass of safe and useful continuations. Model-based checks screen plans during training and responses during interaction, requiring at least one sequence of future response strategies that meets a prescribed safety bound under every candidate user model, independently of the learned network. Strategies are selected directly from learned first-step probabilities, avoiding online plan sampling. We evaluate the approach in simulation against reactive safeguards, filters with and without memory, and alternative planners, using exact computation to validate the learned approximation. We also evaluate relational cue extraction from real user messages in WildChat. To our knowledge, this is the first approach to select conversational replies by anticipating their effects on the user-AI relationship while imposing an explicit model-based safety bound on future response sequences. Results show close agreement with exact planning, lower decision costs at longer horizons, and improved safety-utility trade-offs when protective responses are less effective. The approach balances immediate support with the longer-term effects of repeated interaction. The source code is available at https://github.com/benedettapicano/ANTHROPOMORPHIC_SAFETY_TRAJ.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: An Affordable Vibrotactile Surface for Tactile Figure Recognition: Exploration Strategies of Blind and Sighted Users
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Refreshable tactile displays can make graphics accessible to blind and low-vision people, but high-resolution actuator arrays remain expensive. We study whether a low-cost vibrotactile surface can convey simple figures, and how they are read. Nine participants (four blind; five sighted, tested blindfolded then open-eyed) identified seven figures by touch, with video and timing analysis of their exploration. Blind and blindfolded-sighted readers achieved comparable accuracy, but blind participants were about three times faster, using a continuous, rhythmic "gliding" strategy-reading through motion, whereas sighted participants searched in halting, pause-heavy passes; among the sighted, more pausing accompanied errors. Recognition failures were concentrated in specific figures (a diagonal was misread even with vision), locating the bottleneck in representation rather than resolution. We contribute an empirical characterization of tactile reading strategies and design implications for low-cost refreshable tactile displays and affordable tactile representation.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: EE-Motion: An EEG-based Web Architecture for Live Affective Music Recommendation
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Music listening is intrinsically tied to emotion, which drifts continuously within a single session. Although modern browsers interface with wearable brain-computer interfaces, recommendation systems remain structured around discrete logs and lack the infrastructure to integrate continuous physiological signals. Furthermore, existing affect-aware models rely on static user profiles and offline training, failing to serve anonymous newcomers without model retraining. We present a web platform that resolves both challenges. Pairing with a consumer electroencephalogram (EEG) headband over Web Bluetooth, the system captures live EEG, mapping frontal alpha asymmetry and arousal index to normalized valence-arousal proxy coordinates on Russell's circumplex plane. Driven by these coordinates, an affective adapter unifies structurally diverse recommendation backbones under a shared live scoring mechanism. By parameterizing anonymous visitors through a few favorite tracks, the module recommends tracks conditioned on live proxy coordinates. This demonstrates that real-time EEG-derived control signals can steer recommendations without persistent user tables or model retraining.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Controlling Proactive Multimodal AI: Separating Perception from Participation
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Proactive multimodal AI can watch a user's screen, listen to speech, track interaction, and decide whether to enter unfolding work. Little is known about how people want to control what such AI may perceive and how far it may participate. Informed by a 14-person Wizard-of-Oz study, we built SpotMe, a design probe that senses screen, speech, and interaction; chooses Silence, Ask, or Assist; and lets users separately configure what it may perceive, how far it may participate, and what types of support it may provide. In a 16-person study on a civic dashboard, participants first experienced proactive help, then inspected decisions to act or remain silent, and then configured SpotMe's perception and participation. We found that participants could keep all perception channels available while lowering participation to Ask or Silence; that exposing suppressed decisions made silence interpretable and contestable; and that seeing what SpotMe used led some to change how they clicked, highlighted, and spoke. We contribute an empirical account of inspecting and controlling proactive multimodal AI by decoupling perception from participation.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Plenty to FRET About: From Hazard Analysis to Formal Requirements for Robot-Assisted Dressing
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Understanding requirements for systems involving humans and robots is essential for providing robust evidence that such systems behave correctly. Requirements formalisation approaches such as the Formal Requirements Elicitation Tool (FRET) can support the transition from unstructured natural language to formal representations suitable for verification. In this paper, we formalise 146 hazard-derived natural-language requirements for a Robot-Assisted Dressing (RAD) case study, previously classified using a taxonomy of Human-Robot Teamwork (HRT) requirements. Through an iterative process involving domain-expert clarification, these were represented by 117 unique FRETISH requirements. Formalisation exposed ambiguities, temporal and probabilistic assumptions, and cases where source requirements needed to be decomposed or could be consolidated because they expressed the same formal behaviour. Temporal analysis showed that 70.1% of the unique FRETISH requirements use either immediate-response or ordering constraints (immediately or before), while formalisation also exposed relationships between requirements across HRT taxonomy categories. We further analyse the formal semantics and realisability of the resulting requirements. The results show that HRT classification and formalisation provide complementary views: the taxonomy captures the teamwork concern represented by a requirement, while FRETISH makes the required behaviour explicit. We report practical lessons and limitations of applying FRET to HRT requirements and identify directions for further work.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: An AI-Driven Assistant for Human-Centric Building Digital Twin Systems: Design, Implementation, and Comparative User Evaluation
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Smart buildings generate streams of operational data, yet this richness rarely translates into accessible, decision-ready information for stakeholders who inhabit and manage them. Current Building Digital Twin Systems (BDTS) often remain oriented toward technical specialists and rely on static, one-size-fits-all interfaces. This paper presents the design, implementation, and comparative user evaluation of an AI-driven conversational assistant integrated into a human-centric BDTS for Indoor Environmental Quality monitoring, combined with adaptive information presentation and auto-suggest functionality. The prototype was deployed at New York University Abu Dhabi. A controlled, two-arm, between-subjects, quasi-experimental study with wave-based, non-randomized assignment compared the Baseline interface with the Experimental interface. Results showed significant reductions in task-completion time and perceived workload, while accuracy and usability improved but did not meet the adjusted significance criterion. The study contributes an implemented and empirically evaluated architecture that separates generative interaction from deterministic environmental assessment and coordinates conversational responses with adaptive visual presentation.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 43 pages, 8 figures, 9 tables. Submitted to Developments in the Built Environment

Human-Computer Interaction.title: OAK-Mind: Zero-Training Mental Health Change Inference from Passive Sensing via Knowledge-Grounded Multi-Agent LLMs
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Wearable and smartphone sensors capture behavioral signals associated with mental health, yet inferring mental health outcomes from these signals has traditionally relied on supervised models requiring labeled data and offering limited insight into their predictions. Large language models (LLMs) offer new opportunities to reason over behavioral evidence, but existing LLM-based approaches to passive sensing have largely continued to rely on task-specific fine-tuning or sensor-specific pretraining. In this paper, we introduce OAK-Mind, a zerO-training, multi-Agent, Knowledge-grounded LLM pipeline for inferring mental health changes from passive sensing data. The pipeline organizes sensing data into behavioral dimensions including sleep, physical activity, location mobility, and smartphone use, and orchestrates specialized agents grounded in mental health literature to interpret longitudinal behavioral changes. It synthesizes their assessments and applies questionnaire-based symptom rating to infer changes relative to an individual's baseline assessment with human-readable rationale grounded in observed behavioral patterns and domain knowledge. Across datasets and prediction tasks, while without task-specific training, OAK-Mind achieves comparable or better performance than the most predictive supervised baselines trained on additional labeled samples. It also demonstrate consistent improvement upon direct prompting across four tested LLM backbones. Ablation analyses support the benefits of combining behavioral interpretation with symptom rating, distributing analysis across domain-specific agents, and incorporating domain knowledge. Our findings highlight the potential of knowledge-grounded, multi-agent LLMs for training-free inference of mental health changes from passive sensing data.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: Under review at ACM IMWUT. 30 pages, 4 figures and 6 tables

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Big Brains, Tiny Board: Pupavision, an Agentic Physical AI Instrument for Monitoring Drosophila Pupariation and Lifecycle Transitions
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Many biology experiments are limited by the availability and ease of use of instruments that monitor and record them. For example, the timing of pupariation in the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster, a widely used model organism, can provide biologically relevant information about growth regulation and is often recorded manually. Here, we present Pupavision, a small physical AI instrument built from a single-board Linux computer and a day/night camera for roughly 45 to 75 US dollars in parts. The key idea is that a frontier coding agent runs its agentic harness directly on the tiny board. The model thinks in the cloud, but the agent works on the device. The agent assists image capture, writes code to repair errors, and checks the experiment every day to keep raw data capture reliable. If recording stops, the researcher gets a ping on their mobile phone. A simple deterministic capture service records one image every ten minutes and never depends on the agent. We report a 26-day pilot in a fly incubator (about 3,580 frames), including eleven days in which the agent was logged out and capture continued, and a 51-hour outage whose cause led to the layered design. A researcher-in-the-loop workflow then produces per-vial pupariation curves by tracing selected pupae backward in time from a late reference frame. Future work will validate the assay for lifecycle tracking accuracy against expert-labeled data and expand real-time computer vision analysis. Pupavision offers a blueprint for do-it-yourself agentic instruments that put frontier intelligence on a tiny board, with deterministic code underneath. We present this as an early case study from a pilot lab deployment and contribute lessons learned toward a future where scientific domain experts are empowered by DIY agentic hardware.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Projected Route Cues for Bouldering: Effects of Circular, Linear, and Combined Highlighting on Route Observation and Climbing
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Before attempting a bouldering problem, climbers inspect the route to find its holds and plan their moves, which novices find difficult on walls where many routes overlap. We built a projector-camera system that projects route cues onto the wall and compared three cues: circles on the route holds, limb-colored lines connecting the holds, and both combined. Ninety-six participants, 61 of them first-time climbers, each climbed four routes, one per cue and one without projection, in a Latin-square order. In mixed-effects models, all three cues shortened the time before the first attempt; with circles, its geometric mean fell from 83 s to 39 s. Circles also increased the number of moves made within each trial. Lines led to more use of off-route holds than circles, mainly on routes where such holds lay under the projected lines. Participants preferred the combined cue, although no behavioral advantage of it over circles was detected.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 12 pages, 11 figures, 7 tables. Submitted to ITE Transactions on Media Technology and Applications

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Human-AI Writing as Distributed Cognition: Reassessing Collaborative Writing Theories in the Age of LLMs
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: In this paper, we conduct a structured synthesis of existing theories and frameworks on human-human collaborative writing to assess how co-writing with AI reshapes writing in knowledge work settings, and draw seven insights along with design implications for human-AI collaborative writing tools. Our main argument is that, as we delegate more writing to AI, our cognitive process shifts from the traditional plan/write/review process to a plan/delegate/review process, reshaping the distribution of the cognitive labor between human writers and AI writing tools. To ensure that humans cognitively stay in the loop, we discuss a ``prototyping'' approach, where the writing tool scaffolds a healthier distribution of cognition through rapid, small-scale iterations that keep writers mentally in the loop even when generation is delegated to AI. We aim to bring theoretical grounding and practical guidance to the interaction designs of human-AI collaborative writing, with the goal of balancing automation with cognitive integrity.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Thinking Harder Doesn't Lead to Better Choices: Reasoning Effort Increases the Confidence but Not the Correctness of LLM Shopping Agents
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as autonomous shopping agents that process multimodal product listings (consisting of visual and text data) and recommend purchases on behalf of consumers. Naturally, one might assume that models with more thinking power would make higher-quality purchasing decisions. To test this belief, we ask two questions about such agents: does asking a model to think harder make it choose better products, and does the confidence it reports tell us the likelihood it may be wrong? We benchmark ten frontier models on three product-choice benchmarks built from WebShop, Amazon's SQID and Wayfair's WANDS platforms to see if LLMs with more thinking power actually make better-quality product purchase decisions. Across all three benchmarks, we found that increasing the thinking effort does not increase decision quality in a statistically meaningful way. The same change in thinking effort raises stated confidence at a statistically significant level, so extra thinking buys confidence rather than correctness. We also measure the calibration of these models (how well their reported confidence percentage matches their true correctness percentage) in these tasks and show that most models are not well-calibrated at every effort level. We also find that errors are strongly shared: when one model errs in a task, several others tend to err on that same task. Furthermore, on tasks where several models all err, a large number of them pick the same wrong product.

Software Engineering.title: Operating an Agent-Driven Dataset Factory: Discovery, Construction, and Public Release
Software Engineering.summary: Turning public data into prediction datasets requires connecting source discovery, task definition, construction, and distribution. We deployed Dataset Factory to perform these steps continuously under a standing release policy. Bounded language-model tasks interpret sources, write construction code, and review task meaning; deterministic software manages state, workers, retries, and publication. Over 81.53 hours, the factory published 14 datasets at an estimated recurring operating expenditure of about \$2.74 per publication. The accounting includes failed attempts, inference, workers, and hosting. Separate agents completed prediction experiments on all twelve evaluated releases. Source review nevertheless identified a task whose construction filters contradicted its population declaration. The original reviewer accepted later-record exclusions without reconciling them with the published selection rule. This experience documents an operating source-to-release workflow and shows why successful execution and consumer use need separate checks of task meaning.
Software Engineering.comment: 5 pages, 3 figures. Code and evidence: https://github.com/earino/factory-prospective-study

Software Engineering.title: EmbedGym: Letting Coding Agents Develop and Debug Embedded Firmware Without Physical Hardware
Software Engineering.summary: Modern coding agents perform well on general software benchmarks because they can run code and unit tests in a closed loop. Embedded firmware development, however, breaks this loop: a program that compiles can still fail on real hardware due to pin polarity, bus protocol, timing, or networking bugs that an agent at a text terminal cannot observe. Existing embedded coding agents either skip hardware execution, drive GPIO-only simulators with multi-second delays, or test on physical boards in a static environment. In this paper, we present EmbedGym, an interactive virtual hardware environment that lets coding agents develop and debug embedded firmware without physical hardware. EmbedGym uses instruction-level microcontroller unit (MCU) emulators to execute the same binary that would be flashed onto a physical board, connects them to 41 peripheral models, an analog circuit simulator, and virtual WiFi/Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) endpoints, and exposes an interface for agents to change sensor inputs, press buttons, and inspect hardware states. On top of it, we build EmbedGym-Bench, which consists of 598 tasks across 6 MCU-framework pairs graded by hidden timed test vectors, using a five-stage multi-agent workflow that synthesizes peripheral models and tasks from datasheets and driver libraries. We expose EmbedGym to a coding agent at three levels and evaluate eight models over more than 14K trajectories. Even when compilation succeeds 99.7% of the time, 19.9% of compiled firmwares fail at runtime (up to 73% on individual targets). In contrast, interactive hardware testing in EmbedGym increases pass rates across models by +4.9% to +14.7% (up to +31% on individual targets). Our results also show that an agent with EmbedGym outperforms prior embedded agent frameworks, and lightweight models with EmbedGym match frontier models without it at 30-70x lower cost.

Software Engineering.title: What Should an LLM Know? Knowledge-Guided Warm Starts for Software Optimization
Software Engineering.summary:
Large language models (LLMs) process gigabytes in minutes; human experts work far more slowly. Prior studies that explored combinations of human/AI optimizers ignore this gap. Those studies asked systems or humans to label too many examples (e.g., SynthCore needs over four dozen per trial). Here, we test human and AI knowledge under a budget where evaluation is practical (a few dozen labels or fewer).
  We compare five baselines (random search, RRP, EZR, few-shot prompting, and a budget-matched SynthCore variant) against three ways to give an LLM domain knowledge before it proposes its first configurations: (1) AMP lists the domain's rules, then checks each candidate against them; (2) HKMA adds scouted data or documentation to the prompt; and (3) H-DKP has human experts correct the LLM's rules.
  We find that domain knowledge improves the "start-up" phase of LLM optimization, but only when that knowledge is checked, by the LLM itself or by a human expert. Across 49 datasets, unchecked knowledge did no better than few-shot prompting or EZR. On the other hand, AMP's self-checking variant (AMP-4) reached the best statistical rank in 44 of 49 datasets (budget-matched SynthCore: 23 of 49), and H-DKP did so in 7 of 8 expert studies. These checks cost little: half a cent of LLM calls per trial, or 6 to 10 expert contacts.
  Hence we say LLMs may not need more data, but rather their knowledge needs checking (and checking is cheap).

Software Engineering.title: National and State-Level Approaches to Automated Vehicle Certification: A Comparative Framework for State Operational Governance
Software Engineering.summary: Automated vehicle (AV) deployment in the United States is expanding without a unified federal certification framework, leading to substantial variation in how states authorize and oversee AV testing and deployment. This paper examines how U.S. states regulate Society of Automotive Engineers (SAE) Level 4-5 automated driving systems (ADS), identifies common certification approaches, compares them with international practices, and evaluates the implications for North Carolina's future regulatory strategy. Publicly available state statutes, administrative regulations, agency guidance, and federal policy documents were reviewed. Ten states, selected to capture the range of regulatory approaches, were analyzed using a structured framework covering operational scope, governance and oversight, federal interaction, and implementation outcomes. Certification practices in the European Union, China, Japan, and Australia were reviewed for comparative context. Three state certification models were identified, reflecting increasing regulatory involvement: baseline legal compliance, administrative self-certification with ongoing oversight, and permit-based authorization requiring formal agency review before deployment. North Carolina currently aligns with the baseline compliance model. International frameworks are converging toward scenario-based testing, operational-design-domain-specific approval, safety-case documentation, cybersecurity assurance, and lifecycle oversight, although direct transferability to the U.S. is limited. The paper develops a three-model typology for comparing state AV certification approaches and integrates state practices with international frameworks, providing a consistent basis for evaluating differences in regulatory involvement, governance complexity, and institutional responsibilities across jurisdictions.
Software Engineering.comment: Transportation Research Board Annual Meeting 2027

Software Engineering.title: IH-Benchmark: A Conflict-Centered Benchmark for Instruction-Hierarchy Robustness in Large Language Models
Software Engineering.summary: When a language model receives conflicting instructions from different priority levels, which one does it actually follow? This question lies at the heart of reliable LLM deployment. Existing benchmarks answer this only partially, often focusing on a single hierarchy component or adapting public datasets with limited tool-use coverage. We present IH-Benchmark, a conflict-centered benchmark for instruction-hierarchy robustness across direct System $\succ$ User (S $\succ$ U) conflicts and tool-mediated User $\succ$ Tool (U $\succ$ T) conflicts. We organize tests into seven constraint categories according to the higher-priority requirements under evaluation. Each test is evaluated with a uniform binary pass/fail protocol combining a predicate domain-specific language (DSL) with rubric-based LLM judges. We report category-balanced compliance rates and evaluate non-conflict controls separately. Our evaluation of 32 model configurations over five runs each reveals substantial variation in overall compliance, with scores ranging from 32.9% to 97.8%. Models achieve higher compliance on S $\succ$ U than on U $\succ$ T on average, at 84.6% and 69.6%, respectively. Strong performance on the former track does not guarantee comparable robustness on the latter. Constraint hardening provides a prompt-based defense, but its benefits depend on the model and how conflicting instructions are delivered. Several models also resist unauthorized tool actions more reliably than injected instructions that alter response language or factual content. Together, these results show that high aggregate compliance can conceal weaknesses in specific conflict tracks and instruction requirements. We release IH-Benchmark, including the benchmark corpus, agent simulators, and evaluation harness, at LINK_RELEASE_AFTER_PEER_REVIEW.

Software Engineering.title: Can Coding Agents Write and Transpile Unit Tests
Software Engineering.summary: Coding assistants built on Large Language Models (LLMs) have become a staple of modern software development, increasingly trusted to execute workflows and modernize code end-to-end. Much of this trust rests on passing tests, which are often written by the coding agents themselves. In this work, we examine the ability of these agents to both write reliable tests and translate them between programming languages. We benchmark three popular coding agents, each evaluated with a native frontier model and high reasoning effort. Verifying across a broad suite of metrics, we find that coding agents far exceed human written suites on traditional measures of coverage. This advantage, however, is uneven: agent test quality degrades sharply with project size, and much of the advantage lies in a greater number of written tests. We also show that agentic test translation---while seemingly strong in aggregate---remains inconsistent and unreliable.

Software Engineering.title: Training for sustainable scientific software in the AI era: from code production to scientific stewardship
